extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political philosophy; legislators and lawgivers; general readers of classical political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for lawgivers and students on constructing and evaluating the state, constitutions, and the institutions of political life, with emphasis on the aims of government, qualifications for rulers and citizens, and practical/stable constitutional arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the state (end of the city)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state is 'a community of well-being in families and aggregations of families for the sake of a perfect and self-sufficing life.' The city exists for the highest good, enabling men to live well (happiness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation and constitutional design should be judged by whether they make the good life possible for citizens; the state’s institutions must be oriented toward that final end rather than merely order or security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator as teacher of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator is the proper teacher of virtue: public opinion and social environment educate citizens, so the lawgiver must shape them to express the good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and institutions should be crafted to form the moral character of the community; private education cannot override corrupt public institutions. The legislator's role is pedagogical as much as administrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical experience in constitutional design
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional theory must be grounded in the study of real constitutions and political facts—'careful and sympathetic study of a wide range of facts'—not pure abstract idealism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs ought to incorporate historical and comparative evidence (Aristotle's study of many constitutions) and to adapt ideals to actual circumstances rather than impose unreal utopias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical politics: make the best of imperfect states
rubrics_metrics.description: While an ideal state can be defined, much political work concerns improving, preserving, or making the best of imperfect or perverted constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to the lawgiver should include remedies, stabilising measures, and realistic compromises for defective or mixed regimes rather than only prescriptions for an unreachable perfect state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions differ in kind, not merely in number
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of government (domestic, regal, political, etc.) are not merely distinctions of scale or number but differ in constitution and aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses and designs should attend to structural constitutional differences (principles and aims), not assume that scale alone determines the nature of governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: City/state is natural and prior to the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: The city is a natural production and 'man is by nature a political animal'; the political community precedes the family/individual in the order of ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify institutions by their contribution to the full realization of human nature as social/political (speech, justice), and treat the polis as the proper context for political virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizenship qualification: capacity for pursuit of the good
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens should be those capable of rational deliberation about the good life—leisure and capacity for political reflection are prerequisites for full citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining membership and political rights, prioritize those who can participate in deliberation about ends; be explicit about who is excluded and why (e.g., artisans, slaves, 'barbarians' as described).

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as foundation of constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is the paramount instrument by which the legislator ensures future citizens share the beliefs making the state possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design must include public education policies shaping habits, dispositions, and common moral-political beliefs; neglecting education undermines the constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of political justice: 'tools to those who can use them'
rubrics_metrics.description: Political offices and powers should be distributed to those who are most capable of using them to further the state's end (minimize waste of political ability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess distributions of authority by competence to pursue the constitution's aim: in some states this implies aristocracy, in others mixed arrangements that reflect actual capacities and balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality and rotation of rule ('ruling and being ruled in turn')
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional government ideally involves equality in the sense that citizens rule and are ruled in turn; this institutionalizes a check against abuse of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design mechanisms for shared participation and limits on permanent domination; rotation or mixed institutions can combine efficiency and popular control to reduce tyranny by rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed constitution: balance virtue, wealth, and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: A stable mixed constitution distributes political weight among virtue (merit), wealth, and mere number (the many); stability depends on how these interests are balanced, especially the strength of the middle class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing regimes, aim for a balance that mirrors real social power relations; seek to empower a mediating middle class to stabilize the polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: State as expression of common conception of the good, not force
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of the state is community in pursuit of a common good; the presence of force indicates failure of the state's unity, not its proper basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and institutions should foster agreement about ends; reliance on force or coercion is a symptom of political failure and should be minimized by institutional design that cultivates shared ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of revolution: shifts in class power (military/economic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions arise chiefly from changes in the military or economic strength of classes; stability concerns often amount to preserving the existing constitution in face of class struggle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive constitutional measures should address class tensions, economic imbalances, and shifts in military power; institutional safeguards must consider material as well as moral causes of instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawgiving as expert craft (the lawgiver as 'state doctor')
rubrics_metrics.description: Law-making is a technical, expert task distinct from ordinary politics and administration; the lawgiver is called in to prescribe for an ailing constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appoint or consult knowledgeable designers of constitutions; evaluate proposed reforms for technical coherence and suitability to the state's condition rather than partisan advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not disregard experience in favor of abstract ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideals (like Plato’s Republic) are impracticable if they ignore historical experience; the lawgiver must reconcile ideals with empirical realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize solutions that can be implemented given actual social conditions; use ideals as guides but subject them to empirical validation and adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of power should minimize exploitation by rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Because rulers may use power for private ends, constitutions must include mechanisms (equality, rotation, mixed elements) to prevent subordination of citizens to rulers' private purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design checks and shared decision-making to reduce the risk of rulers converting public office into private advantage; institutional constraints on officeholders are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat sectional interests explicitly in constitutional design
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of power should reflect the strengths of the parties or classes represented (virtue, wealth, numbers); successful constitutions represent existing balances of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating constitutions, consider how well they incorporate and mediate competing sectional interests; neglecting such realities invites instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of household/family in the state
rubrics_metrics.description: The family (master/slave, husband/wife, father/child) is the primary component of the city; household management (provisioning, property, instruments) is part of political economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In designing social and economic institutions, account for household organization, the division between provision and governance, and the role of property and instruments (including servants/slaves in Aristotle's account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery and natural subordination (as argued)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some persons are by nature instruments (slaves) whose excellence is corporeal while their masters possess rational leadership; master/slave relation is described as mutually advantageous in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an evaluative standard in Aristotle's framework—designs that rely on hierarchical, naturalized slavery are supported in the text—but modern readers should treat this as a normative claim of the historical text rather than a contemporary rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech and justice as foundation for political community
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech enables humans uniquely to express what is just and unjust; participation in the perception of good and evil forms the basis of family and city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should cultivate and make possible shared speech and deliberation about justice; political life depends on the communicative capacities that enable citizens to form common judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final cause / teleology in evaluating constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate political institutions according to their final cause (the end they serve): the best government is that which serves the state's true end — the good life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological reasoning: assess whether laws and constitutions serve the highest ends of the polis rather than only instrumental goals; identify instruments versus ends in institutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating people merely as instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The analogy of the legislator as craftsman breaks down because the legislator deals with persons capable of their own ends; the state should not treat citizens merely as tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions must respect that citizens have their own ends; legal design should include participatory rights and recognition of citizen agency rather than pure instrumental management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability criterion: represent the actual balance of power
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution will be stable if it represents the real balance of power among classes; where the middle class is strong the mixed constitution is practicable and stabilising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or creating constitutions, ensure institutional arrangements mirror socio-economic realities and provide stakes to groups whose support is essential for longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political role of virtue vs. material concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Different states conceive the aim of the state differently—some as the apprehension of the good (virtue), others as a complex good needing wealth and equality; the constitutional distribution should reflect the conceived end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the state's fundamental conception of its end (virtue-centered vs. mixed goods) and align institutional designs, eligibility, and incentives with that conception.
